full_judgment:
3. Plaint case, in short, is that plaintiff-bank on 30-4-84 advanced a loan facility by an overdraft of Taka 8 lac in favour of defendant-respondent No. 1, Orbit Enterprise Ltd represented by its managing director respondent No.2. The defendant-respondent No.2 mortgaged the property mentioned in schedule of the plaint with the bank for the purpose of securing payment of said loan but subsequently, as the defendant failed to repay the accumulated loan of Taka 8,15,671.65 plaintiff-bank was constrained to file the suit for realisation of the loan money. The total outstanding upto 11-1-88 was calculated at Taka 9,18,219.65. Hence is the suit. 

 4. The defendant-respondent filed written statement and contested the suit. His case is that after getting a work order to establish electric connection and sanitary works of a building of Bangladesh T &T Board, the plaintiff-bank allowed him the said loan facility. It is further stated in the written statement that after some progress of the work, a dispute cropped up between the defendant- respondent No. 2 and the T &T Board which was ultimately referred to the Arbitration Council. The arbitration council passed an award of Taka 56,78,761 in favour of the respondent and on 30-9- 87 the said award was put to make Rule of the Court before the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka by Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1987. In paragraph 'Uma' of the written statement, the defendant No. 1 categorically stated that within few months' time that the said amount would be realised. In the written statement defendant No.1 admitted the entire liability to be discharged against the plaintiffs claim. 

 5. Upon the above pleadings 3 issues were framed. The plaintiff did not cite any witness and the defendant No. 2 was cited as only defendant witness in the case. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit but did not award the pendente lite interest as prayed by the plaintiff against which this appeal has been preferred by the plaintiff-appellant. 

 6. Mr SA Rahim appearing with Mr Syed Abdus Salam, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant, after taking us through the plaint, written statement, evidence of DW and different exhibits from the record, contends that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in passing the decree without awarding any interest pendente lite in his decree as well as interest till the realisation of installments in two years. Elaborating his submission, the learned Counsel further contends that though the provision of awarding interest under law is a discretionary one but under the facts and circumstances of the present case the learned Court should have awarded the interest as prayed by the plaintiff in the plaint. He also empathically submits that the learned Court below had ample power to pass the decree with interest pendente lite but it failed to consider to pay the decretal with interest pendente lite amount in one installment and thereby committed illegality. 

 7. Be that as it may, we have heard the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff- appellant at length and also gone through the plaint, written statement, deposition of DW 1 and other exhibits carefully. The moot question that falls for consideration by this Division in the instant appeal is, whether the subordinate judge was justified in passing the decree appealed against under the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 8. In the written statement filed on 16-1-90, it has been categorically stated in paragraph 'Ulna" that the respondent (defendant No.1) is expecting to have the Rule of the Court at any time and in his deposition made before the Court on 5-11-90, the defendant, while admitting the loan categorically stated in his chief আমি আরবিট্রেশন করিয়া সাতান্ন লাখ টাকার বেশী পাই. In his cross-examination, he directly admitted the claim of the plaintiff and prayed for soft installments and also exonerating the interest. lf we analyse the two things i.e. the statement given by the defendant in the written statement and his subsequent deposition, it becomes clear that though the defendant got the amount of Taka 57 lac by way of arbitration from T &T Board still he did not repay the loan amount which is only Taka 9,18,219.65. Therefore, we may glean that by not taking into account this aspect of fact, the Court below certainly flouted the settled proposition of law that discretion should be exercised judiciously and not capriciously. This is indeed, a fit case where the court should have awarded interest at a reasonable rate. 

 12. We find that this power of awarding interest by the Court is a discretionary one but the question is, whether this discretionary power of the Court is an unfettered one has to be construed in the light of the facts and circumstances of a particular case. Certainly this discretion, in our view, is to be exercised judiciously and not capriciously. 

 14. In the instant case also as we have already discussed, the Court is left with no choice but to award interest as per law. Since from the evidence on record it is found that defendant-respondent had enough money to repay the loan with interest. This fact displaces the discretion of the Court conferred by section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the matter of granting interest. 

 15. In the case as referred to above discretion was displaced by the apex Court considering section 478 of the Insurance Act, 1938. Here in this case this Division displaces the discretion of granting interest under section 34(1), Civil Procedure Code considering the admitted factual position of the case itself. Thakur vs Amolok, AIR 1963 (Raj) 1993 is also on the same point.
